title: Junk Modelling
strapline: A cereal box, a tube and a big idea — making something from nothing, and fixing it when it flops.
intent: Work through a real design cycle: idea, make, test, adapt — the rocket that won't stand up is the best teacher here
Learn joining as a craft in itself: when tape beats glue, how a hinge works, why a flange holds a tube to a box
Build scissor control on honest materials — tissue that tears, card that fights back, tape that sticks to itself
Discover material properties by using them: what bends, what folds, what's sturdy, what droops when it's wet
Grow a maker's vocabulary — cylinder, joint, hinge, attach, sturdy
Persevere through wonky and feel the pride of "I made this"
implementation: Keep a proper workshop: boxes, tubes and lids sorted and visible, with tape children can tear or cut for themselves
Teach joining techniques deliberately — a masking-tape hinge, a slot, a flange — as small skills children can then choose from
Ask about the plan, but accept that for many children the plan emerges from the making
When it flops, hold back the fix: "what do you think is making it droop?" comes before the sticky-tape rescue
Use workshop vocabulary naturally as you work alongside — cylinder, join, sturdy, attach
Display finished models with the child's own words about them, exactly as dictated
Keep models out for revisiting — tomorrow's addition of wings matters more than today's tidy shelf
key_questions: What will you use to stick those together — tape or glue? What makes you say that?
How could you make the wheels actually turn?
It keeps falling over — what would make the bottom sturdier?
What does your model need next?
How did you get the lid to open and close like that?

impact.text: Younger makers snip into tape and paper and stick with growing control — the fascination is the joining itself.
Children cut along drawn lines and around box panels, and use glue spreaders, hole punches and tape dispensers with real intent.
Children make with a plan — "I'm making a rocket" — and adapt when the tube won't stay on: more tape, a different box, a new design.
Material knowledge grows through use: tissue tears, card folds along a scored line, wet PVA doesn't hold yet but will by home time.
Children talk you through their model — what each part does, how they joined it — using new maker words, and notice clever details in friends' models.
Children stick with a tricky make across the morning, or across days, until it works — and feel the win.
The finished model is carried round the room with visible pride: "I did it — look!"
Older children cut and join with precision and patience — small tabs, neat corners, tape torn to just the right length.

enhancements: A real hole punch, treasury tags and split pins for joints that actually move
Masking tape on wall-mounted dispensers at child height so no one has to ask for tape
A "broken toy surgery" basket — old keyboards, clock parts, wheels — for models that need real components
Photographs of vehicles, buildings and machines pinned at the workshop for children who want a reference
A ramp and a fan for testing: does your car roll, does your boat blow along?
Scissors of graded difficulty and left-handed pairs always in the pot
A "still working on it" shelf so unfinished models survive tidy-up time

playing_exploring: Reclaimed materials carry no instructions — a cereal box holds a hundred possible makes
Children try out joining techniques they've been shown, then invent their own
active_learning: The droop, the wobble and the un-stuck wing invite another go — junk modelling is persistence with a glue stick
creating_thinking: Children choose their own way to solve a joining problem and can say why they chose it
Ideas from one make feed the next: the hinge from yesterday's treasure box turns up on today's crocodile jaw
